label: Chapter 7
title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death

blocks.p: When they had passed this place, they came to the borders of the Shadow of Death; and this valley was longer than the other, and a place most strangely haunted with evil things, as many can testify. But these women and children got through it the better because they had daylight, and because Mr. Great-heart was their guide.

When they had entered this valley, they thought they heard a groaning, as of dying men, a very great groaning. They thought, too, that they heard words of lamentation, as of people in extreme torment. These things made the boys shake, and the women turned pale and wan; but their guide told them to take comfort.

They went on a little further, and thought they felt the ground begin to shake under them, as if some hollow place lay beneath; they heard too a kind of hissing, like serpents, but nothing yet appeared. Then the boys said, “Aren’t we at the end of this dismal place yet?” But the guide told them again to be of good courage and to watch their feet, “or you may,” he said, “be caught in some snare.”

Now James began to feel sick, but I think the cause of it was fear; so his mother gave him some of that cordial she had been given at the Interpreter’s house, and three of the pills Mr. Skill had prepared, and the boy began to revive. So they went on, until they came to about the middle of the valley, and then Christiana said, “I think I see something up ahead on the road before us, a thing of a shape I have never seen before.”
“Mother, what is it?” said Joseph.
“An ugly thing, child; an ugly thing,” she said.
“But, Mother, what is it like?”
“It is like—I can’t tell what,” she said. And now it was only a little way off. “It is close,” she said.

“Well, well,” said Mr. Great-heart. “Let those who are most afraid keep close to me.” So the fiend came on, and the guide went to meet it; but just as it reached him, it vanished from all their sight. Then they remembered what had been said long ago: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” [James 4:7]

They went on, then, a little refreshed; but they had not gone far before Mercy, looking behind her, saw what she took to be something very like a lion, padding after them at a great pace, with a hollow, roaring voice; and every roar it gave made the whole valley echo and their hearts ache, all but the heart of their guide. So it came up; and Mr. Great-heart went behind and put the pilgrims all in front of him. The lion came on fast, and Mr. Great-heart made ready to give it battle. But when it saw that resistance was determined, it too drew back and came no further. [1 Pet. 5:8-9]

Then they went on again, with their guide in front, until they came to a place where a pit had been dug across the whole breadth of the road; and before they could prepare to cross it, a great mist and darkness fell on them, so that they could not see. Then the pilgrims said, “Alas! Now what shall we do?” But their guide answered, “Fear not; stand still, and see what end will be put to this too.” So they stayed there, because their path was blocked. They also thought they now heard more plainly the noise and rushing of the enemies; the fire and the smoke of the pit, too, were much easier to make out.

Then Christiana said to Mercy, “Now I see what my poor husband went through. I have heard much of this place, but I was never here before now. Poor man! He came through here all alone, at night; he had night almost the whole way; and these fiends were busy about him as if they would tear him to pieces. Many have spoken of it, but no one can tell what the Valley of the Shadow of Death means until they come into it themselves. ‘The heart knows its own bitterness, and a stranger does not share its joy.’ To be here is a fearful thing.”

“This is like doing business in great waters,” said Mr. Great-heart, “or like going down into the deep; it is like being in the heart of the sea, like going down to the roots of the mountains; now it seems as if the earth with its bars were around us forever. But let those who walk in darkness and have no light trust in the name of the Lord, and lean on their God. [Isa. 50:10] For my part, as I have told you, I have gone through this valley often, and have been much harder pressed than I am now, and yet you see I am alive. I would not boast, for I am not my own savior; but I trust we shall have a good deliverance. Come, let us pray for light to him who can lighten our darkness, and who can rebuke not only these, but all the Satans in hell.”

So they cried out and prayed, and God sent light and deliverance; for now there was nothing to stop them on their way, no, not even there, where only a moment ago a pit had blocked them. Yet they were not through the valley; so they went on, and were met by great stinks and loathsome smells, to their great distress. Then Mercy said to Christiana, “It is not so pleasant being here as at the gate, or at the Interpreter’s, or at the house where we stayed last.”

“Oh, but,” said one of the boys, “it is not so bad to go through here as it would be to stay here always; and for all I know, one reason we must go this way to the house prepared for us is so that our home will be all the sweeter to us.”
“Well said, Samuel,” said the guide. “You have spoken like a man now.”
“Why, if I ever get out of here,” said the boy, “I think I shall value light and a good road better than I ever did in all my life.”
“We shall be out before long,” said the guide.
So on they went, and Joseph said, “Can’t we see to the end of this valley yet?”

“Watch your feet,” said the guide, “for you will soon be among the snares.” So they watched their feet and went on; but the snares troubled them greatly. Now, when they had come among the snares, they saw a man thrown into the ditch on the left, with his flesh all torn and rent. “That is a man named Heedless, who was going this way,” said the guide. “He has lain there a long time. There was one Take-heed with him when he was taken and killed, but he escaped their hands. You cannot imagine how many are killed around here; and yet men are so foolishly bold as to set out lightly on pilgrimage, and to come without a guide. Poor Christian! It was a wonder he escaped here; but he was loved by his God, and he had a good heart of his own, or he could never have done it.”

Now they drew toward the end of the way; and just there, where Christian had seen the cave as he went by, out came Maul, a giant. This Maul used to ruin young pilgrims with clever arguments; and he called Great-heart by name and said to him, “How many times have you been forbidden to do these things?”
“What things?” said Mr. Great-heart.
“What things!” said the giant. “You know what things. But I will put an end to your trade.”
“But please,” said Mr. Great-heart, “before we fall to it, let us understand what we must fight about.” Now the women and children stood trembling, and did not know what to do.
“You rob the country,” said the giant, “and rob it with the worst of thefts.”
“Those are only generalities,” said Mr. Great-heart. “Come to particulars, man.”
Then the giant said, “You practice the trade of a kidnapper. You gather up women and children and carry them off into a strange country, to the weakening of my master’s kingdom.”

“I am a servant of the God of heaven,” Great-heart replied. “My business is to persuade sinners to repent. I am commanded to do my utmost to turn men, women, and children ‘from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God’; and if this is really the ground of your quarrel, let us fall to it as soon as you like.”

Then the giant came on, and Mr. Great-heart went to meet him; and as he went, he drew his sword, but the giant had a club. So without more ado they fell to it, and at the first blow the giant struck Mr. Great-heart down onto one knee; at that the women and children cried out. But Mr. Great-heart recovered himself, and laid about him with full vigor, and gave the giant a wound in his arm; and so he fought for the space of an hour, to such a pitch of heat that the breath came out of the giant’s nostrils as the heat comes out of a boiling cauldron.
Then they sat down to rest; but Mr. Great-heart gave himself to prayer, and the women and children did nothing but sigh and cry the whole time the battle lasted.

When they had rested and caught their breath, they both fell to it again, and Mr. Great-heart, with a full blow, brought the giant down to the ground. “No, hold, and let me recover,” said the giant; so Mr. Great-heart fairly let him get up. Then at it they went again, and the giant came within a hair of smashing Mr. Great-heart’s skull with his club.

Seeing that, Mr. Great-heart ran at him in the full heat of his spirit and pierced him under the fifth rib; at that the giant began to faint, and could hold up his club no longer. Then Mr. Great-heart followed up his blow, and struck the giant’s head from his shoulders. Then the women and children rejoiced, and Mr. Great-heart praised God for the deliverance he had worked. When this was done, they raised a pillar between them and fastened the giant’s head on it, and wrote beneath, in letters that passersby could read:

v: He who once wore this head was one
he stopped their way, he spared none,
until I came, him to oppose,

blocks.p: Now I saw that they went on to the rise a little way off, which had been built up as a lookout for pilgrims (it was the place from which Christian had his first sight of his brother Faithful); and here they sat down and rested, and here too they ate and drank and made merry, because they had been delivered from so dangerous an enemy. As they sat eating, Christiana asked the guide whether he had come to any harm in the battle.

“No,” said Mr. Great-heart, “except a little on my flesh; and even that, far from being to my loss, is at present a proof of my love to my Master and to you, and shall be a means, by grace, of increasing my reward at last.” [2 Cor. 4]
“But weren’t you afraid, good sir, when you saw him come out with his club?”
“It is my duty to distrust my own ability, so that I may rely on him who is stronger than all.”
“But what did you think when he struck you to the ground at the first blow?”
“Why, I thought that my Master himself was served the same way, and yet it was he who conquered in the end.”

“When you have all thought what you please,” said Matthew, “I think God has been wonderfully good to us, both in bringing us out of this valley and in delivering us from the hand of this enemy. For my part, I see no reason why we should ever distrust our God again, since he has now, and in such a place as this, given us such proof of his love.”
